Lab 4: Regression and Classification Evaluation Metrics¶

Part 1: KNN Classification using Breast Cancer Dataset and Comparison with Regression Metrics¶

Author: AIML Student
OS Version: Windows

Aim¶

  • Implement KNN: Build a K-Nearest Neighbors classifier for breast cancer detection.
  • Optimize: Use $\sqrt{n}$ heuristic, train-test splits, and cross-validation to find the best $K$.
  • Evaluate: Test model performance using Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1 Score, and ROC-AUC.
  • Compare: See how classification metrics stack up against regression metrics from Lab 3.

Environment Setup and Imports¶

We first import the required libraries for data manipulation, scaling, classification, visualization, and metrics evaluation.

Task 1: Data Preparation¶

We load the Breast Cancer dataset, check its structure, handle any missing values, and scale the features.

Why do we scale features in KNN?¶

  • Distance matters: KNN relies on calculating distance between points, like Euclidean distance: $$d(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}) = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^d (p_i - q_i)^2}$$
  • Even playing field: If one feature is measured in thousands (e.g., area) and another in decimals (e.g., smoothness), the large numbers will overpower the small ones.
  • The fix: We use StandardScaler ($\mu=0, \sigma^2=1$) to ensure every feature has equal weight.
In [2]:
# 1.1 Load the Breast Cancer dataset
cancer_data = load_breast_cancer()
X = pd.DataFrame(cancer_data.data, columns=cancer_data.feature_names)
y = pd.Series(cancer_data.target, name="target")

# 1.2 Explore the structure

print(f"Dataset Shape: {X.shape[0]} samples, {X.shape[1]} features")
print(f"Target distribution (Counts):\n{y.value_counts()}")
print(f"Target distribution (Percentages):\n{y.value_counts(normalize=True) * 100}\n")

# 1.3 Check missing values and duplicates
missing = X.isnull().sum().sum()
duplicates = X.duplicated().sum()
print(f"Total Missing Values: {missing}")
print(f"Total Duplicate Rows: {duplicates}\n")

# 1.4 Apply Feature Scaling
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X)
X_scaled_df = pd.DataFrame(X_scaled, columns=cancer_data.feature_names)
print("First 3 rows of scaled features:")
X_scaled_df.head(3)

Task 2: Train-Test Split Analysis¶

We experiment with three different splits: 80:20, 70:30, and 90:10 to see how the model behaves.

Which split is best?¶

  • 90:10 Split: Too few test samples. Even a single mistake drastically swings the accuracy (unstable).
  • 70:30 Split: Good for testing, but leaves less data for the model to learn from (can reduce performance).
  • 80:20 Split: The sweet spot! It perfectly balances a solid training size with a reliable test size.
In [3]:
splits = [(0.2, "80:20"), (0.3, "70:30"), (0.1, "90:10")]
split_results = []

for test_size, name in splits:
    # Use stratify=y to maintain class distribution in splits
    X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
        X_scaled, y, test_size=test_size, random_state=42, stratify=y
    )
    
    # Heuristic K rule
    n_train = len(X_train)
    heuristic_k = int(np.round(np.sqrt(n_train)))
    if heuristic_k % 2 == 0:
        heuristic_k += 1  # ensure odd K to break ties
        
    # Fit model
    knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=heuristic_k)
    knn.fit(X_train, y_train)
    
    # Predict
    y_train_pred = knn.predict(X_train)
    y_test_pred = knn.predict(X_test)
    
    split_results.append({
        "Split Ratio": name,
        "Train Size": len(X_train),
        "Test Size": len(X_test),
        "Heuristic K": heuristic_k,
        "Train Acc": accuracy_score(y_train, y_train_pred),
        "Test Acc": accuracy_score(y_test, y_test_pred),
        "Precision": precision_score(y_test, y_test_pred),
        "Recall": recall_score(y_test, y_test_pred),
        "F1 Score": f1_score(y_test, y_test_pred)
    })

split_analysis_df = pd.DataFrame(split_results)
split_analysis_df

Task 3: KNN Model with Heuristic K Selection¶

3.1 The Square Root Rule¶

  • A great starting point for finding $K$ is $K = \sqrt{n}$ (where $n$ is your training size).
  • For 455 training samples, $\sqrt{455} \approx 21.33$.
  • We round this to 21 (always use an odd number to avoid ties during voting!).

3.2 Tuning the Model¶

We train our model at $K=21$ and then test nearby values (from 16 to 26) to see if we can find an even better fit.

In [4]:
# Base split is 80:20
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X_scaled, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=42, stratify=y
)
n_train = len(X_train)
h_k = int(np.round(np.sqrt(n_train)))
if h_k % 2 == 0:
    h_k += 1

# Define range to plot
k_range = list(range(1, 36))
train_accs = []
test_accs = []

for k in k_range:
    model = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k)
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    train_accs.append(accuracy_score(y_train, model.predict(X_train)))
    test_accs.append(accuracy_score(y_test, model.predict(X_test)))

# Find best K within Heuristic K +- 5 range
k_subset = list(range(h_k - 5, h_k + 6))
subset_test_accs = [test_accs[k-1] for k in k_subset]
best_h_k = k_subset[np.argmax(subset_test_accs)]

print(f"Heuristic K: {h_k}")
print(f"Best K in heuristic range {h_k-5} to {h_k+5}: K = {best_h_k} (Test Acc: {max(subset_test_accs):.4f})")

# Plot Accuracy vs K
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(k_range, train_accs, label="Train Accuracy", marker='o', linestyle="--", color="#1f77b4")
plt.plot(k_range, test_accs, label="Test Accuracy", marker='s', color="#ff7f0e")
plt.axvline(x=h_k, color="red", linestyle=":", lw=2, label=f"Heuristic K = {h_k}")
plt.axvline(x=best_h_k, color="green", linestyle="-.", lw=1.5, label=f"Optimal K in range = {best_h_k}")
plt.title("KNN Classification Accuracy vs. K Value (80:20 Split)")
plt.xlabel("Number of Neighbors (K)")
plt.ylabel("Accuracy")
plt.xticks(range(1, 36, 2))
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("images/accuracy_vs_k.png", dpi=150)
plt.show()

Heuristic K: 21
Best K in heuristic range 16 to 26: K = 18 (Test Acc: 0.9825)

3.3 Distance Metrics & Decision Boundaries¶

Euclidean vs. Manhattan Distance¶

  • Euclidean: Straight-line distance. Great for standard, continuous data but struggles if you have extreme outliers or too many dimensions. $$d(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}) = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^d (p_i - q_i)^2}$$
  • Manhattan: Grid-like (taxicab) distance. Perfect for categorical data or grid-based paths, and it handles outliers much better. $$d(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}) = \sum_{i=1}^d |p_i - q_i|$$

Decision Boundaries (Visualizing K)¶

  • K = 1: Highly jagged boundary. It tries to perfectly fit every single point, which leads to overfitting (capturing noise).
  • K = 5 & 10: Smoother boundaries. It ignores minor noise and captures the real pattern.
  • K = 20: Too smooth. It loses important details and underfits the data.
In [5]:
# PCA projection to 2D
pca = PCA(n_components=2)
X_train_pca = pca.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_pca = pca.transform(X_test)

# Plot decision boundaries
k_vals = [1, 5, 10, 20]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(14, 12))
axes = axes.ravel()

# Create meshgrid
x_min, x_max = X_train_pca[:, 0].min() - 1, X_train_pca[:, 0].max() + 1
y_min, y_max = X_train_pca[:, 1].min() - 1, X_train_pca[:, 1].max() + 1
xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.arange(x_min, x_max, 0.05),
                     np.arange(y_min, y_max, 0.05))

for i, k in enumerate(k_vals):
    knn_pca = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k)
    knn_pca.fit(X_train_pca, y_train)
    
    Z = knn_pca.predict(np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()]).reshape(xx.shape)
    
    # Plot contours
    axes[i].contourf(xx, yy, Z, alpha=0.3, cmap=plt.cm.RdYlBu)
    scatter = axes[i].scatter(X_train_pca[:, 0], X_train_pca[:, 1], c=y_train,
                              cmap=plt.cm.RdYlBu, edgecolor='k', s=30, alpha=0.8)
    
    # Labels and Titles
    train_acc = accuracy_score(y_train, knn_pca.predict(X_train_pca))
    test_acc = accuracy_score(y_test, knn_pca.predict(X_test_pca))
    axes[i].set_title(f"K = {k} | Train Acc: {train_acc:.3f} | Test Acc: {test_acc:.3f}")
    axes[i].set_xlabel("PCA 1")
    axes[i].set_ylabel("PCA 2")
    axes[i].legend(*scatter.legend_elements(), loc="lower left", title="Target")

plt.suptitle("KNN Decision Boundaries in 2D PCA space", y=0.98, fontsize=16)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("images/decision_boundaries.png", dpi=150)
plt.show()

Task 4: Cross-Validation¶

A single train-test split can be "lucky" or "unlucky" depending on how the data was shuffled.

Why Cross-Validation?¶

  • We chop the data into 10 chunks (folds).
  • We train on 9 chunks and test on the 1, rotating until every chunk has been a test set.
  • This gives us a much more reliable and robust estimate of how the model will perform in the real world.
In [6]:
# 10-Fold Cross-Validation Setup
kf = KFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
cv_means = []
cv_stds = []

for k in k_range:
    knn_cv = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k)
    scores = cross_val_score(knn_cv, X_scaled, y, cv=kf, scoring='accuracy')
    cv_means.append(scores.mean())
    cv_stds.append(scores.std())

cv_means = np.array(cv_means)
cv_stds = np.array(cv_stds)

# Find best K from CV
best_cv_idx = np.argmax(cv_means)
best_cv_k = k_range[best_cv_idx]
print(f"Optimal K from 10-Fold CV: K = {best_cv_k} (Mean Accuracy = {cv_means[best_cv_idx]:.4f} ± {cv_stds[best_cv_idx]:.4f})")

# Plot CV results
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(k_range, cv_means, label="Mean CV Accuracy", color="#2ca02c", marker='o')
plt.fill_between(k_range, cv_means - cv_stds, cv_means + cv_stds, alpha=0.15, color="#2ca02c", label="±1 Std Dev")
plt.axvline(x=h_k, color="red", linestyle=":", lw=2, label=f"Heuristic K = {h_k}")
plt.axvline(x=best_cv_k, color="blue", linestyle="-.", lw=1.5, label=f"Optimal CV K = {best_cv_k}")
plt.title("10-Fold Cross-Validation Accuracy vs. K Value")
plt.xlabel("Number of Neighbors (K)")
plt.ylabel("Accuracy")
plt.xticks(range(1, 36, 2))
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("images/cv_accuracy_vs_k.png", dpi=150)
plt.show()

Optimal K from 10-Fold CV: K = 11 (Mean Accuracy = 0.9701 ± 0.0196)

Final K Selection¶

  • We started with a guess of $K = 21$.
  • Our 10-fold cross-validation showed that $K = 11$ actually gives the best and most stable accuracy.
  • $K = 11$ is odd (no ties) and gives excellent generalization, so it becomes our final pick!

Task 5: Classification Evaluation¶

Now we evaluate our winning model ($K = 11$) using the 80:20 split. We will look at Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1 Score, the Confusion Matrix, and the ROC-AUC curve.

Classification Formulas¶

  • Accuracy: $\frac{\text{TP} + \text{TN}}{\text{TP} + \text{TN} + \text{FP} + \text{FN}}$
  • Precision: $\frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FP}}$
  • Recall: $\frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FN}}$
  • F1 Score: $2 \times \frac{\text{Precision} \times \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}}$
In [7]:
# Train final model
final_knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=best_cv_k)
final_knn.fit(X_train, y_train)

y_pred = final_knn.predict(X_test)
y_proba = final_knn.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

# Calculate metrics
acc = accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred)
prec = precision_score(y_test, y_pred)
rec = recall_score(y_test, y_pred)
f1 = f1_score(y_test, y_pred)

print(f"Final Model Metrics (K = {best_cv_k}):")
print(f"Accuracy:  {acc:.4f}")
print(f"Precision: {prec:.4f}")
print(f"Recall:    {rec:.4f}")
print(f"F1 Score:  {f1:.4f}\n")

print("Classification Report:")
print(classification_report(y_test, y_pred, target_names=cancer_data.target_names))

# Confusion Matrix Heatmap
cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred)
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 5))
sns.heatmap(cm, annot=True, fmt="d", cmap="Blues", cbar=False,
            xticklabels=cancer_data.target_names, yticklabels=cancer_data.target_names)
plt.title(f"Confusion Matrix (K = {best_cv_k})")
plt.xlabel("Predicted Label")
plt.ylabel("True Label")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("images/confusion_matrix.png", dpi=150)
plt.show()

# ROC Curve & AUC
fpr, tpr, thresholds = roc_curve(y_test, y_proba)
roc_auc = auc(fpr, tpr)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
plt.plot(fpr, tpr, color='#1f77b4', lw=2, label=f'ROC Curve (AUC = {roc_auc:.4f})')
plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color='gray', linestyle='--')
plt.xlim([-0.02, 1.02])
plt.ylim([-0.02, 1.02])
plt.xlabel('False Positive Rate (1 - Specificity)')
plt.ylabel('True Positive Rate (Recall / Sensitivity)')
plt.title(f'Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Curve (K = {best_cv_k})')
plt.legend(loc="lower right")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("images/roc_curve.png", dpi=150)
plt.show()

Task 6: Comparative Study with Regression (Lab 3 Integration)¶

In Lab 3, we used metrics like MAE, MSE, RMSE, and $R^2$ for Linear Regression. Here is how evaluating regression compares to classification:

The Main Difference¶

  • Regression: Measures how far off our numeric predictions are (error magnitude).
  • Classification: Measures how often we pick the right category (decision correctness).

Metric Match-Up¶

  • $R^2$ Score vs. Accuracy: Both give a quick overall performance percentage, but both can be misleading if data is skewed.
  • RMSE vs. F1 Score: Both give a balanced view. RMSE penalizes huge numeric mistakes, while F1 balances False Positives and False Negatives.
  • MAE vs. Confusion Matrix: MAE shows average error size. A Confusion Matrix shows exactly which categories are getting confused.

Key Takeaways¶

  • Scale vs. Correctness: Regression cares about how big the mistake is. Classification just cares if you picked the wrong category.
  • Accuracy is flawed: If 95% of patients are healthy, guessing 'healthy' every time gives 95% accuracy?but misses 100% of sick patients.
  • Recall is crucial: In medicine, missing a cancer diagnosis (False Negative) is fatal. Recall measures how many sick patients we actually caught.
  • ROC-AUC: Helps find the perfect sweet spot (threshold) for diagnosing between sick and healthy patients.

Task 7: Analytical Questions¶

Q1: Why is KNN a "lazy" learner?¶

  • It doesn't actually "train" a model upfront. It just memorizes the data.
  • All the heavy lifting (calculating distances) happens at the very end when you ask it for a prediction.
    • Training Time complexity: $\mathcal{O}(1)$
    • Inference Time complexity: $\mathcal{O}(n \cdot d)$

Q2: Why scale features?¶

  • KNN uses distance. If features aren't on the same scale, huge numbers will drown out tiny numbers. Scaling levels the playing field.

Q3: What is the $\sqrt{n}$ rule?¶

  • It's a quick trick to find a balanced $K$.
  • Too small captures noise, too big ignores patterns. The square root of your training size is a solid middle ground.

Q4: Single Split vs. Cross-Validation?¶

  • A single split can be biased if the shuffle is weird. Cross-validation tests multiple shuffles and averages the results for a truer score.

Q5: How does K affect bias/variance?¶

  • Small K: Overfits (high variance, low bias). Captures every little noisy detail.
  • Large K: Underfits (low variance, high bias). Too broad and ignores important patterns.

Q6: Why is Recall more important than Accuracy for cancer?¶

  • Accuracy treats all mistakes equally.
  • Recall focuses on False Negatives (missing a cancer diagnosis). In medicine, missing a diagnosis is fatal, so we prioritize Recall above all else. $$\text{Recall} = \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FN}}$$

Q7: What happens if K is huge?¶

  • The model just predicts whatever the most common class is for everything, completely ignoring the actual data features.

Conclusion¶

We built and evaluated a KNN classifier on breast cancer data. Here is what we learned:

  • Finding the best K: We guessed $K=21$ using $\sqrt{n}$, but cross-validation proved $K=11$ was the true winner.
  • The best split: An 80:20 train-test split gave us the perfect balance of training data and testing stability.
  • Stellar Performance: Our final model hit $97.37\%$ accuracy and a perfect $100\%$ Recall?which is exactly what we want in medicine to ensure no sick patient is missed.
  • Regression vs Classification: Regression measures numeric error sizes, while classification measures categorical decision correctness.
